jabal-amil.s: Jabal Amil is a region in southern Lebanon with a long tradition of Shia scholarship. The Safavid Empire imported Arab Shia scholars from Jabal Amil and Bahrain to help convert Iran to Twelver Shia Islam.

jacques-cartier.s: Jacques Cartier was a French explorer who made voyages to North America from 1534. He explored the Gulf of St.

jadwiga-of-poland.s: Jadwiga was crowned ruler of Poland in the late fourteenth century. Under the Union of Krewo of 1385 she married the Lithuanian grand duke Jogaila, who accepted Latin Christianity and became King Władysław II Jagiełło.

jafari-school.s: The Ja'fari school is the main school of Twelver Shia Islamic jurisprudence, named after the imam Ja'far al-Sadiq. In 1736 Nader Shah proposed that it be recognised as a fifth school of law alongside the four Sunni schools.

jagiellonian-dynasty.s: The Jagiellonian dynasty was a royal house that ruled Poland, Lithuania and at times Bohemia and Hungary from the late fourteenth to the late sixteenth century. It began with Jogaila's marriage to Jadwiga in 1386.

jagir.s: A jagir was an assignment of land revenue to an official or military commander in South Asia, typically in return for service. In the Mughal Empire jagirs supported the mansabdars, and were usually transferable rather than hereditary.

jalali-calendar.s: The Jalali calendar is a solar calendar introduced in the late eleventh century under the Seljuk sultan Malik Shah, with the participation of the mathematician Omar Khayyam. It was more accurate than the contemporary Julian calendar.

jalayirid-sultanate.s: The Jalayirid Sultanate was a Mongol-descended dynasty that ruled Iraq and western Iran in the fourteenth century. It emerged from the fragmentation of the Ilkhanate after the death of Abu Sa'id in 1335.

jamaica.s: Jamaica is a Caribbean island that was a British colony from the seventeenth century until 1962, with a plantation economy based on enslaved labour. It adopted the Westminster parliamentary model inherited from the British Empire.

jamestown.s: Jamestown was an English settlement in Virginia founded in 1607. It was the first permanent English colony in North America.

jami.s: Jami was a fifteenth-century Persian poet and Sufi scholar, active in Herat. He is regarded as one of the last great classical Persian poets.

jami-al-tawarikh.s: Jami' al-Tawarikh, or Compendium of Chronicles, is a universal history compiled by Rashid al-Din, vizier of the Ilkhanate, in the early fourteenth century. It covers the Mongols and many other peoples of Eurasia and was richly illustrated.

jan-iii-sobieski.s: Jan III Sobieski was King of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in the late seventeenth century and an accomplished military commander. In 1683 he led the relief army that defeated the Ottoman siege of Vienna.

jan-pieterszoon-coen.s: Jan Pieterszoon Coen was an officer and Governor-General of the Dutch East India Company in the early seventeenth century. He founded Batavia on Java in 1619 as the company's headquarters.

janissaries.s: The Janissaries were the elite infantry corps of the Ottoman Empire, originally recruited from Christian boys through the devshirme system. They became one of the first standing armies in Europe to use firearms on a large scale.

japan.s: Japan is an island nation in East Asia. It absorbed many influences from the Tang Dynasty and resisted the invasions of the Yuan Dynasty, was unified under the Tokugawa Shogunate, and traded with Portuguese and Dutch merchants.

japanese-invasion-of-the-dutch-east-indi.n: Japanese invasion of the Dutch East Indies
japanese-invasion-of-the-dutch-east-indi.s: The Japanese invasion of the Dutch East Indies was a campaign of 1941–1942 in which Japanese forces conquered the Dutch colonial territories in present-day Indonesia, seeking their oil and other resources. The Allied naval forces were defeated in the Battle of the Java Sea.

japanese-tea-ceremony.s: The Japanese tea ceremony is a ritual preparation and serving of powdered green tea, shaped by Zen Buddhist ideals of simplicity and harmony. It was refined by masters such as Sen no Rikyū in the sixteenth century.

japonisme.s: Japonisme was the fashion for Japanese art and design in Europe and America in the later nineteenth century, after Japan opened to the West. Japanese woodblock prints influenced Impressionism, Post-Impressionism and Art Nouveau.

java.s: Java is a densely populated island in Indonesia. It was the heartland of the Majapahit Empire and an important rival or part of the Srivijaya sphere.

java-sea.s: The Java Sea is a shallow sea between Java, Borneo and Sumatra in Indonesia. It was a key maritime trade route used by the Srivijaya and Majapahit empires.

jawhar-al-siqilli.s: Jawhar al-Siqilli was a Fatimid general of Sicilian or slave origin. In 969 CE he led the conquest of Egypt for the Fatimid Caliphate and founded the new city of Cairo.

jayavarman-ii.s: Jayavarman II was a Khmer ruler who in 802 CE proclaimed himself universal monarch, or chakravartin, in a ceremony declaring independence from Java. His reign is traditionally regarded as the foundation of the Khmer Empire.

jayavarman-vii.s: Jayavarman VII was a Khmer king of the late twelfth and early thirteenth century. He drove out Cham invaders who had sacked Angkor and expanded the empire to its greatest extent.

jean-baptiste-colbert.s: Jean-Baptiste Colbert was a minister of Louis XIV of France who directed finance, commerce and the navy. He promoted mercantilist policies, trading companies and colonial development, and built up the French navy.

jean-baptiste-ventura.s: Jean-Baptiste Ventura was an Italian former officer of Napoleon's armies who entered the service of Ranjit Singh. With other European officers he helped train Sikh infantry along European lines.

jean-francois-allard.s: Jean-François Allard was a French former officer of Napoleon's armies who entered the service of Ranjit Singh. He organised and trained cavalry units of the Sikh army on European lines.

jean-jacques-dessalines.s: Jean-Jacques Dessalines was a leader of the Haitian Revolution. After the defeat of the French expedition, he declared the independence of Haiti in 1804 and became its first ruler.

jehoiachin.s: Jehoiachin was a king of Judah who surrendered Jerusalem to Nebuchadnezzar II in 597 BCE. He was deported to Babylon with the Judean elite.

jeronimos-monastery.s: The Jerónimos Monastery is a monastery in Lisbon built from the early sixteenth century in the ornate Manueline style. Its construction was funded by revenues from the spice trade.

jerusalem.s: Jerusalem is an ancient city in the Levant, sacred to Judaism, Christianity and Islam. It was destroyed by the Chaldean Empire, restored under the Achaemenid Empire, and taken by the Sasanian Empire in the seventh century.

jesuits.s: The Jesuits, or Society of Jesus, are a Catholic religious order founded in 1540. They were leading missionaries in Asia, Africa and the Americas.

jews.s: The Jews are a people and religious community descended from the ancient Israelites. Jewish communities lived in many empires, often as protected minorities.

jezzailchi.s: Jezzailchis were soldiers armed with the jezail, a long-barrelled musket used in Iran, Afghanistan and Central Asia. Nader Shah employed mounted infantry armed with firearms who could dismount to deliver accurate musket fire and then remount for pursuit.

jhelum.s: The Jhelum is one of the five rivers of the Punjab, flowing from Kashmir into present-day Pakistan. With the Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, it sustained the intensive agriculture of the region.

jiaozi.s: Jiaozi was a form of paper money that first appeared in Sichuan in the early eleventh century, initially issued by merchants and later taken over by the government. It is generally regarded as the world's first government-issued paper currency.

jiedushi.s: Jiedushi were military governors of the Tang Dynasty, originally appointed to command frontier armies. Over time they gained control of civil administration, taxation and troops in their regions.

jihad.s: Jihad is an Islamic term meaning struggle or striving, which can refer to spiritual effort or to armed struggle in defence or expansion of the faith. Armed jihad was a central theme in the founding of the Sokoto Caliphate and in Saladin's wars against the crusaders in the…

jinchuan-campaigns.s: The Jinchuan campaigns were military expeditions of the Qing Empire in the eighteenth century against the Jinchuan chieftaincies in the mountains of western Sichuan. Fought in difficult terrain against fortified stone towers, they proved extremely costly.

jingkang-incident.s: The Jingkang incident was the capture of the Northern Song capital Kaifeng by Jurchen Jin forces in 1127, in which the retired emperor Huizong and the reigning emperor Qinzong were taken captive. The Song court re-established itself in the south.

jinshi.s: Jinshi was the highest degree in the Chinese imperial examination system, awarded to candidates who passed the metropolitan and palace examinations. Holders were eligible for senior posts in the bureaucracy.

jizya.s: Jizya was a tax levied in Islamic states on non-Muslim subjects, the dhimmi, in return for protection and exemption from military service. It was established in the Rashidun Caliphate and continued in the Umayyad Caliphate, where it was an important source of revenue.

joao-afonso-de-aveiro.s: João Afonso de Aveiro was a Portuguese explorer who reached the kingdom of Benin in the 1480s. His visit led to formal diplomatic and commercial relations between Portugal and Benin under Oba Ozolua.

johann-martin-honigberger.s: Johann Martin Honigberger was a physician from Transylvania who served at the court of Ranjit Singh in Lahore. He later wrote a memoir, Thirty-five Years in the East.

johannes-gutenberg.s: Johannes Gutenberg was a fifteenth-century German craftsman who developed printing with movable metal type in Europe. His press transformed the spread of knowledge in Europe.

johannes-van-den-bosch.s: Johannes van den Bosch was a Dutch Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies. In 1830 he introduced the Cultivation System in Java, which forced peasants to devote part of their land or labour to export crops for the colonial government.

john-i-of-portugal.s: John I of Portugal was the founder of the House of Aviz, who secured the throne after a succession crisis in the late fourteenth century. His reign confirmed Portuguese independence from Castile.

john-ii-of-portugal.s: John II of Portugal was a king of the late fifteenth century who vigorously promoted exploration along the African coast. During his reign Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, and he negotiated the Treaty of Tordesillas with Spain.

john-v-of-portugal.s: John V of Portugal was a king of the first half of the eighteenth century. Gold and diamonds discovered in Brazil funded his extravagant court culture and building projects.

johor.s: Johor is a state at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, which became the seat of a Malay sultanate after the fall of Malacca. Like Malacca, Penang and Singapore, it functioned as a commercial entrepôt.

joint-stock-company.s: A joint-stock company is a business owned by shareholders who invest capital and share in its profits and losses. The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, was an early and influential example with publicly traded shares.

jolof-empire.s: The Jolof Empire was a Wolof state in present-day Senegal that dominated the region from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. It was made up of a confederation of kingdoms under the Buurba Jolof.

jong-ship.s: The jong was a large ocean-going ship of the Javanese and Malay world, capable of carrying large crews and cargoes. Majapahit's naval forces used such ships to transport troops, horses and supplies across the archipelago.

josiah-harlan.s: Josiah Harlan was an American adventurer who travelled to Afghanistan and the Punjab in the early nineteenth century. He was among the foreign officers employed by Ranjit Singh.

judaea.s: Judaea was the region of the southern Levant centred on Jerusalem, the land of the Jewish people in antiquity. Under the Seleucid Empire its Jewish communities initially kept their ancestral law.

judah.s: Judah was an ancient kingdom in the southern Levant with its capital at Jerusalem. It was conquered by the Chaldean Empire under Nebuchadnezzar II.

judaism.s: Judaism is the monotheistic religion of the Jewish people, based on the Hebrew Bible and rabbinic tradition. Its history was shaped by the Assyrian and Chaldean conquests, the Achaemenid restoration and the conflict with the Seleucid Empire.

judar-pasha.s: Judar Pasha was a commander in the service of the Saadi sultan of Morocco, of Spanish origin. In 1591 he led a Moroccan army of about 4,000 soldiers across the Sahara and defeated the Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi using firearms.

jugol.s: The Jugol is the defensive wall of the city of Harar in eastern Ethiopia. It was built under Nur ibn Mujahid in the mid-sixteenth century, after the death of Imam Ahmad.

julian-emperor.s: Julian was a Roman emperor of the fourth century CE, known for attempting to restore traditional paganism. He led a major expedition against Persia but died in the campaign in 363 CE.

julian-calendar.s: The Julian calendar is a solar calendar introduced by Julius Caesar in 46 BCE, with a leap year every four years. It remained the standard calendar in Europe until the Gregorian reform.

julius-caesar.s: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman whose victory in civil war made him dictator, before his assassination in 44 BCE. His intervention in Egypt supported Cleopatra VII, and their relationship drew the Ptolemaic Empire into Roman politics.

july-crisis.s: The July Crisis was the diplomatic crisis of 1914 following the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary issued an ultimatum to Serbia, and alliances drew the great powers into the First World War.

jurchen-jin-dynasty.s: The Jurchen Jin dynasty ruled northern China from 1115 until 1234. It destroyed the Liao and captured the Song capital Kaifeng in 1127.

jurchens.s: The Jurchens were a Tungusic people of Manchuria. In the twelfth century they founded the Jin dynasty, which conquered northern China from the Song Dynasty.

jury-trial.s: Jury trial is a legal procedure in which a panel of citizens decides the facts of a case. In the Russian Empire, Alexander II's Judicial Reform of 1864 introduced trial by jury along with independent courts and adversarial procedure.

justin-i.s: Justin I was a Byzantine emperor of the early sixth century, uncle of Justinian I. According to the site, a major Aksumite naval expedition across the Red Sea was undertaken at his request.

justinian-i.s: Justinian I was a Byzantine emperor of the sixth century CE. He ordered the codification of Roman law later known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, built the Hagia Sophia and reconquered parts of the western Mediterranean.

john-king-of-england.s: John, King of England from 1199, was the youngest son of Henry II. He lost Normandy, Anjou, Maine and Poitou to Philip II of France from 1204, breaking up the Angevin Empire, though the Channel Islands stayed loyal.

john-i-albert.s: John I Albert was a Jagiellonian king of Poland from 1492 to 1501, son of Casimir IV. He strengthened the rights of the nobility in the Sejm and led a failed campaign into Moldavia in 1497.

john-i-of-sweden.s: John I of Sweden, John Sverkersson, was king of Sweden from 1216 to 1222, the last of the House of Sverker. In 1220 he led a Swedish crusade to western Estonia and occupied Lihula, but after he returned home the Oeselians destroyed the garrison he left behind.

john-iii-of-sweden.s: John III of Sweden was a son of Gustav Vasa who received the Duchy of Finland in 1556. His independent foreign policy and marriage to the Polish princess Catherine Jagiellon led his brother Eric XIV to imprison him.

john-iii-duke-of-cleves.s: John III, Duke of Cleves, called the Peaceful, married Maria, heiress of Jülich and Berg. On inheriting from his father and father-in-law by 1521 he united Cleves, Mark, Jülich, Berg and Ravensberg into the United Duchies, a major power of the lower Rhine.

john-iii-duke-of-bavaria.s: John III, Duke of Bavaria, called the Pitiless, was prince-bishop-elect of Liège, where he crushed a rebellion in 1408. After the death of his brother William in 1417 he fought his niece Jacqueline of Hainaut for the inheritance of Holland, Zeeland and Hainaut.

john-iii-count-of-namur.s: John III was the last Count of Namur of the house of Dampierre. Heavily in debt and without legitimate heirs, he sold the county to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, in 1421, keeping its use for life.

john-iii-burgrave-of-nuremberg.s: John III, Burgrave of Nuremberg, was a Hohenzollern prince who in the division of 1398 received the Franconian lands 'above the mountains' around Kulmbach and the Plassenburg, the later principality of Bayreuth. He died without sons in 1420, and his lands passed to his brother…

john-ii-of-france.s: John II, called the Good, was King of France from 1350 to 1364, during the Hundred Years' War. He was captured by the English at Poitiers in 1356 and held in London, while his son, the future Charles V, faced revolt in Paris and the Jacquerie.

john-ii-doukas.s: John II Doukas was ruler of Thessaly from 1303 to 1318, a grandson of John I Doukas, who had made Thessaly a separate principality. He came to power as a minor, looked to Byzantium for support against the Catalan Company and the Duchy of Athens, and married a daughter of…

john-ii-duke-of-bavaria.s: John II was a Wittelsbach Duke of Bavaria who ruled jointly with his brothers Stephen III and Frederick until the partition of 1392 gave him the lands around Munich, creating the Duchy of Bavaria-Munich. After his death in 1397 his sons Ernest and William III ruled jointly.

john-ii-count-palatine-of-simmern.n: John II, Count Palatine of Simmern
john-ii-count-palatine-of-simmern.s: John II was Count Palatine and Duke of Simmern from 1509 to 1557, ruling a small Wittelsbach territory in the Hunsrück together with a share of Sponheim. He introduced the Reformation in his lands and was a patron of learning, supporting a printing press at Simmern.

john-zapolya.s: John Zápolya was Voivode of Transylvania from 1510 and, after the death of Louis II at Mohács in 1526, was elected King of Hungary by the nobles as John I. A rival party elected Ferdinand of Habsburg, and Zápolya turned to the Ottoman sultan Suleiman for support.

john-iii-of-portugal.s: John III was King of Portugal from 1521 to 1557. To defend Brazil against French traders, in 1534 he divided its coast into hereditary captaincies granted to nobles and officials, and when most of them failed he created a central government in 1549 under the governor-general…

joachim-murat.s: Joachim Murat was a French cavalry commander and Marshal of the Empire who married Napoleon's sister Caroline. Napoleon made him Grand Duke of Berg in 1806 and King of Naples in 1808, where he ruled as Joachim Napoleon and introduced French reforms.

john-vi-of-portugal.s: John VI was regent of Portugal from 1799 and king from 1816 to 1826. When Napoleon invaded in 1807 he moved the court to Brazil, opened its ports and in 1815 raised it to a kingdom within the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.

joseph-brant.s: Joseph Brant, Thayendanegea, was a Mohawk military and political leader closely tied to the British through his sister Molly Brant and Sir William Johnson. During the American Revolution he led Mohawk and Loyalist forces against the rebels in New York.

joseph-ii-holy-roman-emperor.s: Joseph II was Holy Roman Emperor from 1765, co-ruler with his mother Maria Theresa, and sole ruler of the Habsburg Monarchy from 1780 to 1790. An enlightened absolutist, he abolished serfdom, granted toleration to Protestants and Jews, closed many monasteries and imposed…

julius-nyerere.s: Julius Nyerere was a Tanzanian teacher and politician who led the Tanganyika African National Union to independence in 1961. He became Prime Minister and then President of Tanganyika, and in 1964 united it with Zanzibar to form Tanzania, which he led until 1985.

john-of-bohemia.s: John of Luxembourg, known as John the Blind, was King of Bohemia from 1310 to 1346. Son of Emperor Henry VII, he gained Bohemia by marriage to Elisabeth of the Přemyslid line and spent much of his reign campaigning abroad.

james-ii-of-england.s: James II of England, also James VII of Scotland, was King of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1685 to 1688. As Duke of York he received New Netherland from his brother Charles II in 1664 and it was renamed New York; as king he created the Dominion of New England.

james-ii-of-cyprus.s: James II of Cyprus was the illegitimate son of King John II. With Mamluk help he ousted his half-sister Queen Charlotte and ruled Cyprus from 1463, taking Famagusta back from the Genoese in 1464.

james-ii-of-majorca.s: James II of Majorca was the younger son of James I of Aragon, who left him Majorca, Roussillon, Cerdanya and Montpellier in 1276. His separate kingdom was squeezed by his brother Peter III of Aragon, who forced him to become a vassal.

james-ii-of-aragon.s: James II of Aragon, called the Just, was King of Aragon from 1291 and earlier King of Sicily. In 1297 Pope Boniface VIII granted him the new Kingdom of Sardinia and Corsica, and his son Alfonso conquered the Pisan parts of Sardinia in 1323 and 1324.

joachim-ernest-prince-of-anhalt.s: Joachim Ernest, Prince of Anhalt, reunited all the Anhalt lands under his rule in 1570 and issued a common law code for them. He was a Lutheran prince who maintained a strong court at Dessau.

joachim-ernst-duke-of-anhalt.s: Joachim Ernst was the last Duke of Anhalt, succeeding as a minor in September 1918. His regent abdicated on his behalf in November 1918 during the German Revolution, and the duchy became the Free State of Anhalt.

johann-sebastian-bach.s: Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer and organist, born at Eisenach. He held posts at the small courts and towns of central Germany, including Arnstadt, Weimar and Köthen, where he wrote much of his instrumental music, before becoming cantor at Leipzig in 1723.

john-hunyadi.s: John Hunyadi was a Hungarian general and nobleman of Wallachian origin who led the fight against the Ottomans. He was voivode of Transylvania from 1441, ban of Severin and regent of Hungary from 1446 to 1453.

john-william-duke-of-julich-cleves-berg.s: John William was the last Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, ruling from 1592. He suffered from mental illness, and his court was torn by factions.

jose-de-san-martin.s: José de San Martín was an Argentine general who led the liberation of southern South America from Spain. He led the Army of the Andes across the mountains into Chile, where with Bernardo O'Higgins he won at Chacabuco in 1817 and Maipú in 1818.

juan-ponce-de-leon.s: Juan Ponce de León was a Spanish conquistador who began the conquest of Puerto Rico in 1508 and became its first governor. In 1513 he led the first known European expedition to Florida and gave it its name.

juba-ii.s: Juba II was the son of King Juba I of Numidia, raised in Rome after his father's defeat by Julius Caesar. Augustus made him client king of Mauretania in 25 BCE, and he married Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Cleopatra and Mark Antony.

james-brooke.s: James Brooke was an English adventurer who helped the Brunei Sultanate put down a revolt near Kuching and in 1841 was made Rajah of Sarawak. He founded the dynasty of the White Rajahs, which ruled Sarawak for a century.

james-cook.s: James Cook was a British naval officer who led three voyages of exploration in the Pacific between 1768 and 1779. He charted New Zealand and eastern Australia, visited Tahiti and the Society Islands, named New Caledonia in 1774 and reached Hawaii in 1778.

jacques-dyel-du-parquet.s: Jacques Dyel du Parquet was a nephew of Pierre Belain d'Esnambuc and governor of Martinique from 1637. In 1649 he landed settlers on Grenada and built a fort at the site of St George's, and in 1650 he sent settlers to Saint Lucia.

jahan-shah-qara-qoyunlu.s: Jahan Shah was ruler of the Qara Qoyunlu Turkoman confederation from 1438 to 1467, governing from Tabriz. At first a vassal of the Timurid Shah Rukh, he expanded his state after 1447 over Iraq, western and central Iran, and briefly took Herat in 1458.

james-douglas-governor.s: James Douglas was a Hudson's Bay Company fur trader and chief factor who founded Fort Victoria in 1843. He governed the Colony of Vancouver Island from 1851 to 1864, concluding the Douglas Treaties with First Nations, and in 1858 also became governor of the new Colony of…

james-i-of-aragon.s: James I, called the Conqueror, was king of Aragon and count of Barcelona from 1213 to 1276. He conquered Majorca in 1229 and the Muslim kingdom of Valencia in 1238, creating new realms with their own laws within the Crown of Aragon.

jan-van-riebeeck.s: Jan van Riebeeck was a Dutch East India Company official who landed at Table Bay in 1652 to set up a station supplying fresh food to ships sailing to the East Indies, the beginning of Cape Town. He commanded the Cape until 1662, when he became governor of Malacca until 1665.

jani-beg.s: Jani Beg was khan of the Golden Horde from 1342 to 1357, son of Uzbek Khan. During his siege of the Genoese port of Caffa in 1346 plague broke out among his army, and ships from Caffa may have carried the Black Death towards Europe.

jason-of-pherae.s: Jason of Pherae was tyrant of Pherae in Thessaly who built a large mercenary army and forced Pharsalus, under Polydamas, to submit. Elected tagos, the federal leader of Thessaly, around 374 BCE, he made Thessaly briefly a great power, allied with Thebes and was said to plan a…

jassa-singh-ahluwalia.s: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia was a Sikh leader who became supreme commander of the Dal Khalsa, the combined Sikh forces, from 1748, and head of the Ahluwalia misl. The Sikhs fought the Mughal governors and the invasions of Ahmad Shah Durrani under his leadership, and he briefly held…

jawaharlal-nehru.s: Jawaharlal Nehru was a leader of the Indian National Congress in the struggle for independence and a close associate of Mahatma Gandhi, imprisoned many times by the British. He became the first prime minister of India in 1947 and held office until his death.

jean-pierre-boyer.s: Jean-Pierre Boyer was president of Haiti from 1818 to 1843. After Henri Christophe's death in 1820 he reunited the north with the republic, and in 1822 he occupied Santo Domingo, ruling all of Hispaniola until 1844.

johann-reinhard-iii-of-hanau.s: Johann Reinhard III was the last count of Hanau, ruling Hanau-Lichtenberg from 1680 and also Hanau-Münzenberg from 1712. A builder and patron of the arts, he governed lands on the Main and in Alsace.

john-i-count-of-nassau-weilburg.s: John I was count of Nassau-Weilburg from the partition of 1344, ruling lands of the Walramian line of the house of Nassau south of the Lahn. Through his marriage to Johanna, heiress of Saarbrücken, he gained that county for his family, and in 1366 the emperor Charles IV raised…

john-i-duke-of-mecklenburg-stargard.s: John I was a son of Henry II of Mecklenburg. In 1348 he and his brother Albert II were raised by the emperor Charles IV from lords to dukes of Mecklenburg, and in their division of 1352 John received the eastern Lordship of Stargard, around Neubrandenburg.

john-i-of-gaeta.s: John I was hypatus, or ruler, of Gaeta in the early 10th century, succeeding his father Docibilis I, founder of the dynasty. He joined the alliance of Pope John X, Byzantium and the southern Italian princes that destroyed the Saracen colony on the Garigliano in 915, and he…

john-louis-prince-of-nassau-hadamar.s: John Louis was a son of John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg who received Hadamar in the division of his father's lands in 1607. He converted to Catholicism in 1629 and brought his territory back to the Catholic faith, serving the emperor as a diplomat, notably at the negotiations for…

john-mason-connecticut.s: John Mason was an English soldier who settled in Connecticut and commanded its forces in the Pequot War. In May 1637, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, he attacked the fortified Pequot village at Mystic and set it on fire, killing hundreds of men, women and children.

john-mason-governor.s: John Mason was an English sea captain and colonial promoter who governed the Newfoundland colony at Cuper's Cove from 1615 to about 1621. In 1622 he and Sir Ferdinando Gorges received the land between the Merrimack and Kennebec rivers, and after they divided it in 1629 Mason…

john-of-ibelin-the-old-lord-of-beirut.n: John of Ibelin, the Old Lord of Beirut
john-of-ibelin-the-old-lord-of-beirut.s: John of Ibelin, the Old Lord of Beirut, was a half-brother of Queen Isabella I of Jerusalem and the most powerful baron of the crusader states in his time. He received Beirut after its recovery in 1197, rebuilt its citadel and a celebrated palace, and served as regent of…

john-of-ibelin-count-of-jaffa.n: John of Ibelin, Count of Jaffa and Ascalon
john-of-ibelin-count-of-jaffa.s: John of Ibelin, Count of Jaffa and Ascalon, was a nephew of the Old Lord of Beirut and the leading jurist of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. His treatise on the laws and customs of the High Court, part of the Assizes of Jerusalem, is the largest legal work of the crusader states.

john-of-ibelin-lord-of-arsuf.n: John of Ibelin, Lord of Arsuf
john-of-ibelin-lord-of-arsuf.s: John of Ibelin, Lord of Arsuf, was a son of John of Ibelin, the Old Lord of Beirut. He held Arsuf, served as constable of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and acted several times as bailli, or regent, for its absent Hohenstaufen kings in the 1240s and 1250s.

john-troglita.s: John Troglita was a Byzantine general sent by Justinian I to North Africa in 546, after Berber revolts and army mutinies had shaken the new Praetorian Prefecture of Africa. In campaigns from 546 to 548 he defeated the Laguatan and the Moorish leader Antalas, restoring…

john-winthrop-the-younger.s: John Winthrop the Younger was the son of the Massachusetts governor John Winthrop. In 1635, as governor for the patentees led by Lord Saye and Sele and Lord Brooke, he sent men to build a fort at the mouth of the Connecticut River, the start of Saybrook Colony.

jose-antonio-paez.s: José Antonio Páez was a cattle-plains leader whose llanero cavalry fought for Venezuelan independence under Simón Bolívar, winning at Las Queseras del Medio in 1819 and sharing the victory of Carabobo in 1821. Commanding in Venezuela within Gran Colombia, he led the Cosiata…

jose-gervasio-artigas.s: José Gervasio Artigas led the rising of the Banda Oriental against Spanish Montevideo in 1811 and became leader of the Eastern Province. Demanding independence and a federal union, he broke with Buenos Aires and in 1814–1815 drew the provinces of the Littoral into the Federal…

joseph-gallieni.s: Joseph Gallieni was a French army officer and colonial administrator who commanded in the Upper Senegal and Niger region of French Sudan in the 1880s and served in Tonkin. As governor-general of Madagascar from 1896 to 1905 he abolished the Merina monarchy in 1897, exiled…

jovan-nenad.s: Jovan Nenad was a Serbian leader who, after the Ottoman victory at Mohács in 1526, gathered an army of Serbs in the southern Hungarian plain and proclaimed himself tsar, ruling from Subotica over much of Bačka and the Banat. In the contest for the Hungarian throne he turned…

jovan-uglesa.s: Jovan Uglješa was a Serbian magnate who, with the title of despot, ruled the region of Serres in eastern Macedonia from about 1365, after the Serbian Empire of Stefan Dušan began to break up. With his brother King Vukašin of Prilep he led a campaign against the Ottomans in…

juan-manuel-de-rosas.s: Juan Manuel de Rosas was a rancher and Federalist caudillo who governed Buenos Aires from 1829 to 1832 and from 1835 to 1852 with extraordinary powers, directing the foreign affairs of the Argentine Confederation. He dealt with frontier peoples through campaigns, treaties and…

juqu-mengxun.s: Juqu Mengxun was a Lushuihu Xiongnu chief who rebelled against Later Liang in 397 and set up the official Duan Ye as ruler of Northern Liang, then killed him in 401 and ruled himself. He made Guzang his capital in 412, destroyed Western Liang by 421, flooding Dunhuang, and…

johann-von-munchhausen.s: Johann von Münchhausen was a Livonian churchman of a Lower Saxon noble family who held the bishoprics of Ösel-Wiek and Courland. At the outbreak of the Livonian War in 1559 he sold both to Frederick II of Denmark and returned to Germany.

jacob-kettler.s: Jacob Kettler was Duke of Courland and Semigallia from 1642 to 1682, a vassal of Poland-Lithuania. Influenced by mercantilist ideas, he built ironworks, shipyards and a large merchant fleet, and founded colonies on the Gambia River and on Tobago, making Courland one of the…

john-george-elector-of-brandenburg.s: John George was Elector of Brandenburg from 1571 to 1598, a Hohenzollern prince and strict Lutheran. In 1571 he inherited both the electorate and the Neumark of his uncle John of Küstrin, reuniting the Brandenburg lands.

john-george-i-elector-of-saxony.n: John George I, Elector of Saxony
john-george-i-elector-of-saxony.s: John George I was Elector of Saxony from 1611 to 1656. A Lutheran loyal to the emperor, he helped crush the Bohemian revolt and gained Lusatia, but later joined Sweden before making the Peace of Prague in 1635.

jabal-al-druze.s: Jabal al-Druze is a volcanic upland in southern Syria, around Suwayda, settled mainly by Druze from the 18th century. Under the French mandate it formed a separate Druze state from 1921.

jacqueline-countess-of-hainaut.s: Jacqueline of Bavaria, of the House of Wittelsbach, inherited Hainaut, Holland and Zeeland in 1417. Her claims were contested by her uncle John of Bavaria and her cousin Philip the Good of Burgundy in a long war.

jadeja.s: The Jadeja are a Rajput clan who ruled Kutch from the 16th century and spread into Saurashtra. In 1540 Jam Rawal founded Nawanagar, and other branches held Rajkot, Gondal, Morvi, Malia, Kotda Sangani and many smaller states.

jagat-singh-of-kullu.s: Jagat Singh was a Raja of Kullu in the upper Beas valley in the 17th century. He expanded the kingdom and moved the capital to Sultanpur, the present town of Kullu.

jagat-singh-of-nurpur.s: Jagat Singh was a Pathania Raja of Nurpur in the Punjab hills, son of Raja Basu. He served the Mughals as a commander, including campaigns in Afghanistan, but rebelled against Shah Jahan in 1641–1642.

jai-singh-prabhakar.s: Jai Singh Prabhakar was Maharaja of Alwar in Rajputana from 1892. Gifted and well educated, he became notorious for erratic and cruel rule.

james-butler-1st-earl-of-ormond.s: James Butler, 1st Earl of Ormond, was head of the Anglo-Norman Butler family, hereditary butlers of Ireland. In 1328 he was created Earl of Ormond and granted palatine rights over Tipperary, giving the earls their own courts and officials.

james-augustus-grant.s: James Augustus Grant was a Scottish army officer and explorer who accompanied John Hanning Speke on the expedition of 1860–1863 to find the source of the Nile. In 1861 the pair stayed with King Rumanyika I of Karagwe, and their accounts made the kingdom known in Europe.

james-grant-british-army-officer.s: James Grant was a Scottish army officer who served as the first governor of British East Florida from 1764 to 1771, after Spain ceded Florida in 1763. He tried to attract settlers with land grants and encouraged indigo and rice plantations.

jan-smuts.s: Jan Smuts was a South African statesman who fought as a Boer general and then, with Louis Botha, led the Het Volk party in the Transvaal Colony and negotiated union in 1910. He was prime minister of the Union of South Africa in 1919–1924 and 1939–1948, served in the British…

javad-khan.s: Javad Khan of the Ziyadoghlu Qajar line was the last khan of Ganja, ruling from 1786. He supported Agha Muhammad Khan Qajar against Georgia in 1795.

jebel-marra.s: Jebel Marra is a volcanic massif in Darfur, western Sudan, rising to about 3,000 metres. Its well-watered slopes supported farming and dense settlement in an arid region, and it was the heartland of successive Darfur states: the Daju, the Tunjur and the Keira sultans of…

jigme-singye-wangchuck.s: Jigme Singye Wangchuck was the fourth King of Bhutan, reigning from 1972 to 2006. He promoted the idea of Gross National Happiness and protected traditional culture and the environment while modernising slowly.

jivaji-rao-puar.s: Jivaji Rao Puar was a Maratha commander who, with his brother Tukoji Rao, came to Malwa with the Peshwa Baji Rao I and received Dewas around 1728. Their shared holding developed into two princely states, and Jivaji Rao was the founder of the Junior Branch, Dewas Junior, which…

joao-goulart.s: João Goulart was a Brazilian labour politician who became president in 1961 after Jânio Quadros resigned, accepted by the military only under a temporary parliamentary system. His proposals for land reform and ties to the left alarmed the military, the middle classes and the…

john-de-courcy.s: John de Courcy was an Anglo-Norman knight who invaded Ulster in 1177, captured Downpatrick and defeated the king of the Ulaid. He ruled eastern Ulster almost independently from Carrickfergus and Downpatrick, building castles and founding monasteries.

john-ii-the-good.s: John II the Good was the last Piast duke of Opole in Upper Silesia, who also gained Racibórz in 1521. He issued a charter of privileges for Upper Silesia and encouraged mining at Tarnowskie Góry.

john-iii-doukas-vatatzes.s: John III Doukas Vatatzes was emperor of Nicaea from 1221. He promoted agricultural self-sufficiency, restricted luxury imports and founded charities.

john-iv-duke-of-brittany.s: John IV, Duke of Brittany, of the House of Montfort, won the War of the Breton Succession by defeating and killing his rival Charles of Blois at the Battle of Auray in 1364. Recognised as duke by the Treaty of Guérande in 1365, he balanced between England and France and…

john-iv-laskaris.s: John IV Laskaris became emperor of Nicaea as a boy in 1258. His regent and co-emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered Constantinople in 1261 and then had John blinded and confined, ending the Laskarid dynasty.

john-iv-of-portugal.s: John IV of Portugal, the eighth Duke of Braganza, was proclaimed king on 1 December 1640 when Portuguese nobles rose against Spanish rule in Lisbon. Founder of the Braganza dynasty, he fought the Restoration War against Spain and recovered Brazil and Angola from the Dutch.

john-sigismund-zapolya.s: John Sigismund Zápolya was the son of John Zápolya, king of eastern Hungary, and Isabella Jagiellon, elected king as an infant in 1540 under Ottoman protection. He ruled from Gyulafehérvár and supported the Diet of Torda's decree of religious freedom in 1568.

john-vi-kantakouzenos.s: John VI Kantakouzenos was a Byzantine statesman who fought the civil war of 1341–1347 against the regency for John V Palaiologos, relying on Turkish allies such as Umur Bey of Aydin and the Saruhanids. He ruled as emperor from 1347 to 1354, made his son Manuel despot of the…

john-vi-count-of-nassau-dillenburg.s: John VI, Count of Nassau-Dillenburg, was a brother of William the Silent and a leading Calvinist prince who organised the Union of Utrecht of 1579 as stadtholder of Gelderland. He founded the academy at Herborn.

jomo-kenyatta.s: Jomo Kenyatta was a Kikuyu nationalist leader imprisoned by the British during the Mau Mau emergency. As leader of the Kenya African National Union he became prime minister at independence on 12 December 1963 and president when Kenya became a republic in 1964.

joscelin-ii-of-edessa.s: Joscelin II was the last count of Edessa, succeeding his father Joscelin I in 1131. While he was absent, Imad al-Din Zengi took the city of Edessa on 24 December 1144, which prompted the Second Crusade.

jose-nunez-de-caceres.s: José Núñez de Cáceres was a Dominican lawyer and official who, frustrated by Spanish neglect, led a bloodless coup in Santo Domingo on 1 December 1821. He proclaimed the Independent State of Spanish Haiti and sought union with Gran Colombia.

jose-santos-zelaya.s: José Santos Zelaya was a Liberal president of Nicaragua from 1893 to 1909. He modernised the state, separated church and state and incorporated the Mosquito Reserve in 1894.

joseph-jenkins-roberts.s: Joseph Jenkins Roberts was a free-born African American merchant from Virginia who emigrated to Liberia in 1829. He became the first Black governor of the Commonwealth of Liberia in 1841 and, after independence was declared on 26 July 1847, the republic's first president.

josip-broz-tito.s: Josip Broz Tito led the Communist Partisans against the Axis occupation of Yugoslavia, setting up his first headquarters at Užice in 1941. He ruled socialist Yugoslavia from 1945 until his death, broke with Stalin in 1948, developed workers' self-management and helped found…

jozef-pilsudski.s: Józef Piłsudski was a Polish revolutionary who led the Polish Legions in the First World War and sat on the Provisional Council of State in 1917 before being interned by the Germans. In November 1918 he took power in Warsaw as chief of state of the new Second Polish Republic,…

juan-bosch.s: Juan Bosch was a Dominican writer and politician who founded the Dominican Revolutionary Party in exile during the Trujillo dictatorship. He won the first free elections after Trujillo's death in December 1962 but was overthrown by a military coup in September 1963.

juan-de-esquivel.s: Juan de Esquivel was a Spanish conquistador who crushed the Taíno rising in Higüey, in eastern Hispaniola, in 1503–1504, capturing the cacique Cotubanamá. In 1509 Diego Colón sent him to occupy Jamaica, where he founded Sevilla la Nueva on the north coast and became the…

juan-jose-flores.s: Juan José Flores was a Venezuelan-born general of the independence wars who governed the southern district of Gran Colombia. When it broke away in 1830 as Ecuador, he became the new republic's first president and annexed the Galápagos Islands in 1832.

juan-sanchez-ramirez.s: Juan Sánchez Ramírez was a Dominican creole landowner who led the revolt against French rule in Santo Domingo after Napoleon's invasion of Spain. He defeated General Ferrand at Palo Hincado in November 1808 and, with British naval help, took Santo Domingo in 1809.

jura-beg.s: Jura Beg was a beg of the Kenagas Uzbek tribe who, with Baba Beg, held Shahrisabz in the Qashqadarya valley independent of the Emirate of Bukhara in the mid-19th century. Russian forces took Shahrisabz in 1870 and handed it to Bukhara.

justinian-ii.s: Justinian II was a Byzantine emperor of the Heraclian dynasty who reigned from 685 to 695 and again from 705 to 711. In 688 he agreed with the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik to share the revenues of Cyprus, and he campaigned against the Slavs of the Strymon, resettling many in…

james-the-great.s: James the Great, son of Zebedee, was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, executed in Jerusalem by Herod Agrippa I around 44 CE. Medieval tradition held that his body had been carried to Galicia, and the discovery of his supposed tomb at Compostela in the early 9th century,…

jibla.s: Jibla, also called Dhu Jibla, is a town in the highlands of Yemen, south of Ibb. Around 1087 Queen Arwa al-Sulayhi made it the capital of the Sulayhid dynasty, building a palace and the great mosque that holds her tomb.

joseph-i-holy-roman-emperor.s: Joseph I, Holy Roman Emperor, of the Habsburg dynasty, reigned from 1705 to 1711 during the War of the Spanish Succession. After the allied victory at Blenheim he placed the Bavarian and Cologne electors under the imperial ban and confiscated or redistributed their lands,…

june-revolution-albania.s: The June Revolution was an uprising in Albania in June 1924 that drove Ahmet Zogu from power and brought the Orthodox bishop and reformer Fan Noli to the head of the government. Noli promised land reform and democratic change but failed to win foreign recognition or hold…

jaan-anvelt.s: Jaan Anvelt was an Estonian Bolshevik leader who chaired the Commune of the Working People of Estonia, proclaimed in Narva in November 1918 with Soviet Russian backing during the Estonian War of Independence. After the Commune collapsed in 1919 he directed the communist…

jaan-poska.s: Jaan Poska was an Estonian lawyer and statesman, mayor of Reval (Tallinn), who became commissar of the Autonomous Governorate of Estonia created in 1917 after the February Revolution. He later served in the provisional government of the Republic of Estonia, and as head of the…

jabala-ibn-al-ayham.s: Jabala ibn al-Ayham was the last king of the Ghassanids, the Christian Arab allies of the Byzantine Empire on the Syrian frontier. He led Ghassanid forces for Byzantium against the Rashidun Caliphate, including at the Battle of the Yarmuk in 636.

jacinda-ardern.s: Jacinda Ardern is a New Zealand politician of the Labour Party who was prime minister from 2017 to 2023. She gained international attention for her response to the Christchurch mosque shootings of 2019, after which her government tightened gun laws, and for New Zealand's…

jacob-sturm.s: Jacob Sturm was a statesman of the free imperial city of Strasbourg who led its government and diplomacy for three decades. He guided the city's adoption of the Reformation in the 1520s alongside the reformer Martin Bucer, represented it at imperial diets, and was a leading…

jacobo-arbenz.s: Jacobo Árbenz was a Guatemalan army officer and politician who was president of Guatemala from 1951 to 1954. A leader of the revolution of 1944, he carried out a land reform that expropriated uncultivated land of large estates, including that of the United Fruit Company.

jacopo-malaspina.s: Jacopo Malaspina was marquis of Massa, a member of the Malaspina family of Lunigiana, who in 1473 bought Carrara with its marble quarries, uniting Massa and Carrara under one lord. The combined state later passed by marriage to the Cybo family and became the Duchy of Massa and…

jacques-peirotes.s: Jacques Peirotes was a socialist politician and mayor of Strasbourg from 1918 to 1929. A member of the German Reichstag before the war, he took charge of the city during the revolution of November 1918, when soldiers' councils and an Alsatian national council competed for…

jacques-pronis.s: Jacques Pronis was a French agent of the Compagnie de l'Orient who in 1643 established a trading post in south-east Madagascar. He founded Fort-Dauphin, named after the future Louis XIV, in the lands of the Antanosy.

jacques-francois-de-brouillan.s: Jacques-François de Brouillan was a French officer and colonial governor, governor of Plaisance (Placentia) in Newfoundland from 1691 to 1701 and later of Acadia. At Plaisance he oversaw Fort Saint-Louis and the cod fishery, defended the colony against English attacks and took…

jacques-joseph-fabry.s: Jacques-Joseph Fabry was a politician of the Prince-Bishopric of Liège and a leader of the Liège Revolution of 1789. With Jean-Rémy de Chestret he headed the patriot government that took control of the city after the prince-bishop fled, proclaiming the rights of citizens.

jean-remy-de-chestret.s: Jean-Rémy de Chestret was a nobleman of Liège and, with Jacques-Joseph Fabry, a leader of the Liège Revolution of 1789. Serving as burgomaster, he helped govern the patriot regime that took power after the prince-bishop fled and sought the support of Prussia.

jafar-pishevari.s: Ja'far Pishevari was an Iranian Azerbaijani communist who led the Azerbaijan People's Government, set up in Tabriz in 1945 under Soviet occupation. A veteran of the Gilan Soviet Republic and long imprisoned under Reza Shah, he founded the Azerbaijan Democratic Party in…

jafar-qoli-khan-donboli.s: Jafar Qoli Khan Donboli was khan of Khoy in north-western Iran, of the Kurdish Donboli family, who succeeded his father Ahmad Khan after his murder in 1786. He resisted the rising power of Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, and after the Qajars took control of the region he fled north…

jafar-qulu-khan-nakhchivanski.s: Jafar Qulu Khan Nakhchivanski was a member of the family of the former khans of Nakhichevan who led the short-lived Republic of Aras, proclaimed in November 1918 in Nakhichevan and neighbouring districts. The republic aimed to block the territorial claims of the First Republic…

jagat-raj.s: Jagat Raj was a Bundela Rajput ruler, a son of Maharaja Chhatrasal of Bundelkhand. When Chhatrasal died in 1731 his realm was divided between his sons and the Maratha Peshwa, and Jagat Raj received the eastern share centred on Jaitpur, while his brother Hirde Sah took Panna.

jagatjit-singh.s: Jagatjit Singh was maharaja of Kapurthala, a Sikh princely state in Punjab, from 1877 to 1947. A widely travelled Francophile, he built the Jagatjit Palace modelled on Versailles and became known for his lavish court and European marriages.

jager-afrikaner.s: Jager Afrikaner was a leader of the Oorlam Afrikaners, a Khoekhoe group of the Cape frontier who had adopted horses, guns and Cape Dutch. Outlawed after killing a farmer, he led raids from beyond the Orange River before converting to Christianity under the London Missionary…

jagmal-singh.s: Jagmal Singh was the founder of Banswara, a Rajput princely state in southern Rajasthan. A son of Rawal Udai Singh of Dungarpur, who was killed fighting alongside Rana Sanga at the Battle of Khanwa in 1527, he received the eastern part of his father's lands across the Mahi river.

jahan-pahlavan.s: Jahan Pahlavan was the Eldiguzid atabeg of Azerbaijan from 1175 to 1186, son of the dynasty's founder Eldiguz. As guardian of the Seljuk sultan Tughril III, he held the real power in western Iran, ruling Azerbaijan, Arran and much of the Jibal from Hamadan.

jair-bolsonaro.s: Jair Bolsonaro is a Brazilian right-wing politician and former army captain who was president of Brazil from 2019 to 2022. His presidency was marked by conflict with the courts and the press, rising deforestation in the Amazon and a contested response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

jakob-sprenger.s: Jakob Sprenger was a Nazi politician who served as Gauleiter of Hesse-Nassau and, from 1933, as Reich governor of the People's State of Hesse. He oversaw the Nazi takeover of the state's government and the persecution of its Jewish communities, among them the old communities…

jalal-al-din-ahsan-shah.s: Jalal al-Din Ahsan Shah was the founder of the Madurai Sultanate in southern India. Governor of the Delhi Sultanate's province of Ma'bar, he rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughluq in 1335 and declared independence, striking coins in his own name.

jalal-al-mulk-ali.s: Jalal al-Mulk Ali was the emir of Tripoli in Lebanon from 1072 to 1099, of the Shia Banu Ammar family of qadis. He extended the family's rule along the Levantine coast and kept Tripoli independent by balancing between the Seljuks and the Fatimids.

jam-ghulam-qadir-khan.s: Jam Ghulam Qadir Khan was the last ruling Jam of Las Bela, a princely state on the coast of Balochistan, who acceded to Pakistan in March 1948. After Las Bela joined the Baluchistan States Union and then West Pakistan, he remained a leading figure in Balochistan politics and…

jam-nizam-al-din-ii.s: Jam Nizam al-Din II, known as Jam Nindo, was the most celebrated ruler of the Samma dynasty of Sindh, reigning from about 1461 to 1508 from Thatta. He is remembered as a just and pious ruler who defended Sindh against the Arghuns of Kandahar.

jam-rawal.s: Jam Rawal was a Jadeja Rajput chief from Kutch who founded the state of Nawanagar in Saurashtra. Around 1540 he conquered the Halar region and founded the town of Nawanagar, the 'new town', later called Jamnagar after the dynasty's title of Jam.

jam-sataji.s: Jam Sataji was ruler of Nawanagar in Saurashtra from 1569 to 1608, a descendant of the state's founder Jam Rawal. He sheltered Muzaffar Shah III, the last sultan of Gujarat, against the Mughals, which led to the Battle of Bhuchar Mori in 1591, and afterwards submitted to…

jamaica-labour-party.s: The Jamaica Labour Party is one of Jamaica's two main political parties, founded in 1943 by the trade unionist Alexander Bustamante, who led it to victory in the first elections under universal suffrage in 1944. Bustamante became the country's first prime minister at…

jamal-al-din-khan-of-talysh.s: Jamal al-Din Khan, called Qara Khan, was the founder of the Talysh Khanate on the south-western shore of the Caspian. Around 1747, after the death of Nader Shah, he made the Talysh district an independent khanate, with its capital first at Astara and then at Lankaran.

jamalul-kiram-ii.s: Jamalul Kiram II was the last sultan of Sulu to hold temporal power, reigning from 1894 to 1936 over the sultanate in the southern Philippines. He signed the Bates Treaty with the United States in 1899, and in 1915, under the Carpenter Agreement, he gave up political authority…

james-hall-colonial-agent.s: James Hall was an American physician and colonisation agent who led the first settlers of the Maryland State Colonization Society to West Africa in 1834. He bought land at Cape Palmas from Grebo rulers and founded the settlement of Harper, the beginning of Maryland in Africa,…

james-iii-of-majorca.s: James III was king of Majorca from 1324 to 1344, ruling the Balearic Islands, Roussillon and the lordship of Montpellier. His cousin Peter IV of Aragon seized his kingdom in 1343–1344 and absorbed it into the Crown of Aragon.

james-mitchell-vincentian-politician.s: James Mitchell, known as Son Mitchell, was a Vincentian politician and agronomist who was prime minister of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines from 1984 to 2000. Founder of the New Democratic Party, he had earlier served as premier in 1972–1974 before independence.

james-murray-governor-of-quebec.s: James Murray was a British Army officer who served under James Wolfe at the capture of Quebec in 1759 and defended the city in 1760. He became military governor of Quebec and, from 1764, the first civil governor of the British Province of Quebec.

james-oglethorpe.s: James Oglethorpe was an English soldier, member of Parliament and philanthropist who founded the colony of Georgia. In 1732 he led the board of Trustees that obtained a charter for the land between the Savannah and Altamaha rivers, intended as a refuge for the poor and a…

james-stewart-lockhart.s: James Stewart Lockhart was a British colonial official and sinologist who served in Hong Kong for many years and was commissioner of the leased territory of Weihaiwei in northern China from 1902 to 1921. He governed lightly through village headmen and Chinese custom, and was…

james-vi-and-i.s: James VI and I was king of Scotland as James VI from 1567 and king of England and Ireland as James I from 1603 until his death in 1625. The son of Mary, Queen of Scots, he inherited the English crown on the death of Elizabeth I, joining the crowns of the two kingdoms in the…

james-wright-governor.s: James Wright was the last royal governor of the Province of Georgia, serving from 1760. Under him rice plantations worked by enslaved Africans spread along the coast, and Georgia's frontier was extended by land cessions from the Creek and Cherokee.

jamshid-khan-of-gilan.s: Jamshid Khan was the last ruler of the Ishaqid dynasty of Fuman in western Gilan, on the Caspian coast of Iran. A relative by marriage of the Safavid shahs, he was deposed when Shah Abbas I conquered Gilan in 1592.

jan-abraham-christian.s: Jan Abraham Christian was kaptein of the Bondelswarts, a Nama community in the far south of German South West Africa. In 1903 he was shot dead by German officials during a dispute over the arrest of a tribesman, and his killing sparked the Bondelswarts rising.

jan-conny.s: Jan Conny was an Ahanta merchant and chief on the Gold Coast who served as an agent of the Brandenburg African Company at Gross Friedrichsburg. When Prussia sold its posts to the Dutch in 1717, he refused to hand over the fort and held it against the Dutch West India Company…

jan-hus.s: Jan Hus was a Czech priest and reformer, rector of the University of Prague, whose criticism of church abuses drew on the ideas of John Wycliffe. Summoned to the Council of Constance under a safe-conduct from King Sigismund, he refused to recant and was burned at the stake…

jan-ii-the-mad.s: Jan II the Mad was a Piast duke of Żagań and Głogów in Silesia, notorious for his violent and unpredictable rule. He sold the Duchy of Żagań to the Wettin rulers of Saxony in 1472, and later fought a long war over the Głogów inheritance, which ended with his expulsion in 1488.

jan-janszoon.s: Jan Janszoon was a Dutch privateer from Haarlem who converted to Islam after his capture by Barbary corsairs and became the corsair captain known as Murat Reis. Based at Salé, he served as a leading figure of the corsair Republic of Salé in the 1620s.

jan-jonker-afrikaner.s: Jan Jonker Afrikaner was the last leader of the Oorlam Afrikaners in central Namibia, a son of Jonker Afrikaner. He took over after his brother Christian was killed fighting the Herero in 1863, as Herero power under Maharero grew.

jan-matthys.s: Jan Matthys was a Dutch Anabaptist preacher, originally a baker from Haarlem, who proclaimed himself a prophet of the coming end of the world. In 1534 he led radical Anabaptists in taking over the city of Münster, which he declared the New Jerusalem, expelling those who…

john-of-leiden.s: John of Leiden, born Jan Beukelszoon, was a Dutch Anabaptist leader, a tailor from Leiden, who ruled Münster during the Anabaptist rebellion. After the death of Jan Matthys in 1534 he proclaimed himself king of the New Jerusalem, introducing polygamy and common property.

jan-sierada.s: Jan Sierada was a Belarusian politician who became the first chairman of the Rada of the Belarusian People's Republic, proclaimed independent in March 1918 under German occupation. The republic never controlled much territory, and he later lived in Soviet Belarus, where he was…

jang-bahadur-rana.s: Jang Bahadur Rana was a Nepalese general and statesman who seized power after the Kot massacre of 1846 and founded the Rana regime, under which his family held hereditary office as prime ministers while the kings were figureheads. He visited Britain and France in 1850, issued…

jangir-khan.s: Jangir Khan was khan of the Bukey Horde, the Kazakh Inner Horde between the Volga and Ural rivers, from 1823 until his death. The son of its founder Bukey, he ruled under Russian protection, built a capital at Khan Ordasy, opened a school and encouraged trade fairs.

jani-khan-qashqai.s: Jani Khan was the paramount chief of the Qashqai, the Turkic-speaking nomadic confederation of the Fars province of southern Iran. The son of Jani Agha, who rose to prominence under Karim Khan Zand, he was recognised by the Qajar shah Fath Ali Shah as ilkhan of the Qashqai in…

janis-cakste.s: Jānis Čakste was a Latvian lawyer and statesman who was the first president of Latvia, serving from 1922 until his death in 1927. A member of the Russian State Duma before the First World War, he chaired the People's Council that proclaimed Latvian independence in November…

janos-kadar.s: János Kádár was a Hungarian communist leader who headed the country from 1956 to 1988. Installed by the Soviet Union after it crushed the revolution of 1956, he oversaw harsh reprisals, including the execution of Imre Nagy.

janusz-ii-of-plock.s: Janusz II was a Piast duke of Masovia who ruled the Duchy of Płock. He was the last duke of the Płock line, and on his death without heirs in 1495 King John I Albert incorporated his duchy into the Kingdom of Poland.

janusz-iii-of-masovia.s: Janusz III was the last Piast duke of Masovia, ruling jointly with his elder brother Stanisław. Both brothers died young, Stanisław in 1524 and Janusz in 1526, amid rumours of poisoning.

jaromar-i-of-rugen.s: Jaromar I was prince of Rügen, ruler of the Slavic Rani on the Baltic island of Rügen. After King Valdemar I of Denmark and Bishop Absalon captured the temple fortress of Arkona in 1168, the Rani princes accepted Christianity and Danish overlordship.

jasper-tudor.s: Jasper Tudor was a Welsh nobleman, half-brother of Henry VI and earl of Pembroke, who was a leading Lancastrian commander in the Wars of the Roses. He protected his nephew Henry Tudor, born at Pembroke Castle in 1457, and shared his exile in Brittany.

jassim-bin-muhammad-al-thani.s: Jassim bin Muhammad Al Thani was ruler of Qatar from 1878 to 1913 and is regarded as the founder of the modern state. Balancing between the Ottoman Empire and Britain, he defeated an Ottoman force at the Battle of al-Wajbah in 1893, confirming his family's authority over the…

jaswant-singh-of-marwar.s: Jaswant Singh was the Rathore ruler of Marwar, with its capital at Jodhpur, from 1638 to 1678 and a senior commander of the Mughal Empire. He served Shah Jahan and later Aurangzeb, campaigning in the Deccan and on the north-west frontier, where he died.

jaswant-singh-of-nabha.s: Jaswant Singh was raja of Nabha, one of the Phulkian Sikh states of Punjab, from 1783 to 1840. In 1809 he placed Nabha under British protection with the other Cis-Sutlej states, keeping it safe from Ranjit Singh's expanding Sikh Empire.

java-war.s: The Java War was a rebellion in central Java from 1825 to 1830 led by Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta against Dutch colonial rule and the Javanese courts that cooperated with it. Fuelled by peasant grievances, Islamic sentiment and Dutch interference, it was fought as a…

jawan-mard-khan.s: Jawan Mard Khan, born Kamal-ud-din Khan Babi, was a Mughal officer in Gujarat of the Babi family of Pathans, which also founded Junagadh State. As Mughal authority collapsed he contested Ahmedabad with the Marathas, and after they took the city in 1753 he secured Radhanpur and…

jaya-prakash-malla.s: Jaya Prakash Malla was the last Malla king of Kantipur (Kathmandu), ruling with interruptions from 1736 to 1768. His reign was troubled by quarrels with his nobles and with the other Malla kingdoms of the valley, while Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha blockaded the valley.

jayabhata-iv.s: Jayabhata IV was the last known king of the Gurjara dynasty of Nandipuri, which ruled the Lata region of southern Gujarat. Known from copper-plate grants, he fought the Arab raids from Sindh in the 730s.

jayachamarajendra-wodeyar.s: Jayachamarajendra Wodeyar was the last maharaja of Mysore, reigning from 1940. He acceded to India in 1947 and served as Rajpramukh of Mysore State from 1950 and then as governor of Mysore and of Madras.

jayasimha-siddharaja.s: Jayasimha Siddharaja was a king of the Chaulukya dynasty of Gujarat who ruled from Anahilavada (Patan) from 1092 to 1142. He defeated the Paramaras of Malwa and extended Chaulukya power to its height.

jayasthiti-malla.s: Jayasthiti Malla was a king of the Malla dynasty of the Kathmandu valley in Nepal, ruling from Bhaktapur from about 1382 to 1395. He reunited the valley after a period of division and is remembered for codifying caste and social rules among the Newars.

jean-de-brebeuf.s: Jean de Brébeuf was a French Jesuit missionary who worked among the Huron (Wendat) from 1626, learning their language and writing a dictionary and catechism. He also visited the Neutral confederacy in 1640–1641.

jean-parisot-de-valette.s: Jean Parisot de Valette was a French knight who was Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller from 1557 to 1568. He led the defence of Malta during the Great Siege of 1565, when the knights and Maltese held out for four months against a large Ottoman army until a relief force…

jean-le-vasseur.s: Jean Le Vasseur was a French Huguenot engineer who took control of the Caribbean island of Tortuga in 1640 on behalf of the French governor of Saint Kitts. He built the Fort de la Roche above Basse-Terre harbour and repelled a Spanish attack in 1643.

jean-moulin.s: Jean Moulin was a French prefect and hero of the Resistance. Sent by Charles de Gaulle into occupied France, he united the main internal resistance movements and in May 1943 founded the National Council of the Resistance, which recognised de Gaulle's leadership.

jean-ribault.s: Jean Ribault was a French Huguenot naval officer who led French attempts to colonise Florida. Backed by Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, he explored the coast in 1562 and left a garrison at Charlesfort, in present-day South Carolina.

jean-bertrand-aristide.s: Jean-Bertrand Aristide is a Haitian former Catholic priest and politician who became Haiti's first democratically elected president in 1990. A champion of the poor and critic of the Duvalier legacy, he was overthrown by a military coup in 1991 and restored by a US-led…

jeanne-dalbret.s: Jeanne d'Albret was queen of Navarre from 1555 to 1572 and sovereign of Béarn, the daughter of Henry II of Navarre and Marguerite of Angoulême. She converted to Calvinism, made it the official religion of Béarn and became a leading figure of the Huguenot cause in the French…

jebel-akhdar-war.s: The Jebel Akhdar War was a conflict in Oman between the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman and the Ibadi Imamate of Oman in the interior, led by Imam Ghalib ibn Ali. Disputes over oil exploration led Sultan Said bin Taimur, backed by Britain, to occupy Nizwa in 1955.

jehudi-ashmun.s: Jehudi Ashmun was an American religious reformer who served as the agent of the American Colonization Society in the colony of Liberia from 1822 to 1828. He organised the defence of the young settlement at Monrovia against attacks by neighbouring peoples and expanded its trade…

jerome-bonaparte.s: Jérôme Bonaparte was the youngest brother of Napoleon, who made him king of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813, with Kassel as his capital. His kingdom received the first written constitution in Germany, abolished serfdom and introduced the Napoleonic Code, but was burdened by…

jeronimo-de-albuquerque.s: Jerónimo de Albuquerque was a Portuguese nobleman in Brazil, the brother-in-law of Duarte Coelho, first donatary of the Captaincy of Pernambuco. He governed the captaincy for long periods during the absence and minority of its heirs, fighting the Indigenous peoples and…

jeronimo-de-albuquerque-maranhao.s: Jerónimo de Albuquerque Maranhão was a Portuguese-Brazilian commander, son of Jerónimo de Albuquerque of Pernambuco and a Tabajara mother. In 1614 he led the expedition against the French colony of Equinoctial France in Maranhão and defeated the French at the Battle of…

jesko-von-puttkamer.s: Jesko von Puttkamer was a German colonial administrator who served as governor of Kamerun from 1895 to 1907. He expanded German control into the interior and promoted concession companies and plantations on the slopes of Mount Cameroon, worked with forced labour.

jesus-de-cardenas.s: Jesús de Cárdenas was a Mexican lawyer and federalist politician who was named president of the Republic of the Rio Grande in January 1840, when federalist leaders in Tamaulipas, Nuevo León and Coahuila declared independence from the centralist government. The republic existed…

jhala.s: The Jhala are a Rajput clan of western India whose chiefs ruled several princely states of Kathiawar in Gujarat, notably Dhrangadhra, Wankaner, Limbdi and Sayla, as well as Jhalawar in Rajasthan. The region of Jhalawad in north-eastern Kathiawar takes its name from them.

jigme-dorje-palbar-bista.s: Jigme Dorje Palbar Bista was the last king of Mustang, a small Tibetan Buddhist kingdom in northern Nepal, reigning from 1964 to 2008. Mustang was a vassal of Nepal, and its king kept a ceremonial role and his palace at Lo Manthang.

jigme-khesar-namgyel-wangchuck.s: Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck is the fifth Druk Gyalpo, king of Bhutan, who succeeded on the abdication of his father Jigme Singye Wangchuck in December 2006. His coronation took place in 2008, the year Bhutan held its first parliamentary elections and adopted a written…

jivajirao-scindia.s: Jivajirao Scindia was the last ruling maharaja of Gwalior, reigning from 1925. He acceded to India in 1947 and in 1948 became Rajpramukh of Madhya Bharat, the union of Gwalior, Indore and the smaller states of Malwa, serving until it merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

joachim-ii-hector.s: Joachim II Hector was elector of Brandenburg from 1535 to 1571, of the Hohenzollern dynasty. On his father's death the Hohenzollern lands were divided, with his brother John receiving the Neumark.

joachim-vadian.s: Joachim Vadian, born Joachim von Watt, was a Swiss humanist scholar, physician and reformer from St. Gallen.

joao-ribeiro.s: João Ribeiro Pessoa was a Brazilian priest and naturalist, a leader of the Pernambucan Revolt of 1817. Influenced by Enlightenment ideas, he joined the provisional republican government in Recife that proclaimed freedom of conscience and the press.

joaquin-ascaso.s: Joaquín Ascaso was a Spanish anarchist of the CNT who presided over the Regional Defence Council of Aragon, created in October 1936 during the Spanish Civil War. The council organised agricultural collectives and supplies for the Aragon front.

joaquin-balaguer.s: Joaquín Balaguer was a Dominican politician and writer who served as president of the Dominican Republic three times: in 1960–1962, from 1966 to 1978 and from 1986 to 1996. A former aide of the dictator Rafael Trujillo, he defeated Juan Bosch in 1966 and ruled for twelve years…

jobst-of-moravia.s: Jobst of Moravia was margrave of Moravia from 1375 and a member of the Luxembourg dynasty, a nephew of Emperor Charles IV. Rich and ambitious, he took part in the struggles among the Luxembourgs and acquired Brandenburg in 1388.

jodh-singh-of-kalsia.s: Jodh Singh was a Sikh chief of the Karorsinghia misl who enlarged the holdings of his father Gurbakhsh Singh south of the Sutlej and made Chhachhrauli the family's seat, founding the state of Kalsia. A noted soldier, he fought in the campaigns of the Sikh chiefs and later…

johan-maurits-of-nassau-siegen.s: Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen was a Dutch count, later prince, who governed Dutch Brazil for the Dutch West India Company from 1637 to 1644. He built Mauritsstad beside Recife, restored sugar production, tolerated Catholics and Jews, and seized Portuguese slave-trading posts…

johann-adolf-i-prince-of-schwarzenberg.n: Johann Adolf I, Prince of Schwarzenberg
johann-adolf-i-prince-of-schwarzenberg.s: Johann Adolf I was the first prince of Schwarzenberg, a senior adviser of Emperor Leopold I and president of the Imperial Aulic Council. In 1670 he was raised to the rank of prince of the Empire, with the family's Franconian lands around Scheinfeld forming the core of the…

johann-adolf-i-duke-of-saxe-weissenfels.n: Johann Adolf I, Duke of Saxe-Weissenfels
johann-adolf-i-duke-of-saxe-weissenfels.s: Johann Adolf I was duke of Saxe-Weissenfels from 1680 to 1697, a member of the Albertine branch of the Wettin dynasty. He succeeded his father Augustus, the founder of the line, and completed the ducal residence of Neu-Augustusburg at Weissenfels.

johann-adolf-ii-duke-of-saxe-weissenfels.n: Johann Adolf II, Duke of Saxe-Weissenfels
johann-adolf-ii-duke-of-saxe-weissenfels.s: Johann Adolf II was the last duke of Saxe-Weissenfels, ruling from 1736 to 1746. A field marshal in the Saxon army, he commanded Saxon forces in the War of the Austrian Succession and was defeated by the Prussians at Hohenfriedberg in 1745.

johann-conrad-von-gemmingen.s: Johann Conrad von Gemmingen was prince-bishop of Eichstätt from 1595 to 1612. A keen collector, he laid out a celebrated botanical garden at his residence, the Willibaldsburg above Eichstätt.

johann-michael-fischer.s: Johann Michael Fischer was a Bavarian architect, one of the leading builders of the south German Baroque and Rococo. Based in Munich, he designed or rebuilt dozens of churches and monasteries, using centralised plans and bright, unified interiors.

johann-wilhelm-duke-of-saxe-eisenach.s: Johann Wilhelm, Duke of Saxe-Eisenach, ruled the small Ernestine duchy from 1698 to 1729. His court at Eisenach kept a notable musical establishment, with Georg Philipp Telemann as Kapellmeister, in the town where Johann Sebastian Bach was born.

johannes-bugenhagen.s: Johannes Bugenhagen was a Pomeranian theologian, close colleague of Martin Luther and pastor of Wittenberg, known as Doctor Pomeranus. He wrote church ordinances for many north German cities and for Denmark.

johannes-kabin.s: Johannes Käbin was an Estonian communist, raised in Russia, who served as First Secretary of the Communist Party of Estonia from 1950 to 1978. He led Soviet Estonia through the post-Stalin decades of industrialisation, oil shale development and large-scale Russian-speaking…

johannes-kepler.s: Johannes Kepler was a German astronomer and mathematician, born in the imperial city of Weil der Stadt, who discovered the three laws of planetary motion. He served as imperial mathematician in Prague and published the Rudolphine Tables in 1627.

johannes-van-walbeeck.s: Johannes van Walbeeck was a Dutch navigator and commander of the Dutch West India Company. In 1634 he led the expedition that captured Curaçao from Spain, giving the company a naval base, salt pans and a foothold close to the Spanish Main.

john-of-saxony.s: John of Saxony was king of Saxony from 1854 to 1873. A scholar as well as a monarch, he translated Dante's Divine Comedy into German under the pen name Philalethes.

john-a-macdonald.s: John A. Macdonald was a Scottish-born Canadian lawyer and Conservative politician, a leader of the Great Coalition of 1864 in the Province of Canada and the main architect of Confederation.

john-albert-ii-duke-of-mecklenburg.n: John Albert II, Duke of Mecklenburg
john-albert-ii-duke-of-mecklenburg.s: John Albert II, Duke of Mecklenburg, shared rule of Mecklenburg with his brother Adolf Frederick I, and their partition of 1621 created the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Güstrow. Both brothers were deposed in 1628 when the emperor gave Mecklenburg to Albrecht von Wallenstein during the…

john-aleman.s: John Aleman was the last lord of Caesarea in the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, holding the lordship through his marriage to its heiress Margaret. In 1265 the Mamluk sultan Baybars captured Caesarea after a short siege and razed its walls, ending the lordship.

john-brown-russwurm.s: John Brown Russwurm was a Jamaican-born American abolitionist and one of the first African American college graduates, from Bowdoin College in 1826. He co-founded Freedom's Journal, the first African American newspaper, in 1827.

john-calvin.s: John Calvin was a French theologian and reformer whose Institutes of the Christian Religion became a founding text of Reformed Protestantism. He arrived in Geneva in 1536, was expelled in 1538 and returned in 1541, writing the church ordinances and working with the Consistory…

john-campbell-missionary.s: John Campbell was a Scottish minister who twice inspected the London Missionary Society's stations in southern Africa. In 1813 he helped the people at Klaarwater adopt a written constitution and renamed the place Griquatown.

john-clarkson.s: John Clarkson was a British naval officer and abolitionist, brother of Thomas Clarkson. For the Sierra Leone Company he organised the voyage of about 1,100 Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia to West Africa in 1792, where they founded Freetown.

john-compton.s: John Compton was a Saint Lucian lawyer and politician who led the United Workers Party and became the first prime minister when Saint Lucia gained independence from Britain on 22 February 1979. He had earlier led the island's government as chief minister and premier, and…

john-endecott.s: John Endecott was an English Puritan who led the advance party of the Massachusetts Bay Company to Salem in 1628. After John Winthrop's arrival he remained a leading magistrate and served as governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony for more years than anyone else, including…

john-ernest-iv-duke-of-saxe-coburg-saalf.n: John Ernest IV, Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld
john-ernest-iv-duke-of-saxe-coburg-saalf.s: John Ernest IV, Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, was the seventh son of Ernest the Pious of Saxe-Gotha. He received Saalfeld in 1680, and after the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg died out in 1699 he gained much of Coburg, founding the line of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld.

john-forrest.s: John Forrest was an Australian explorer, surveyor and politician who crossed the western deserts in the 1870s. When Western Australia gained responsible government in 1890 he became its first premier, serving until 1901 through the gold rushes at Coolgardie and Kalgoorlie.

john-gabalas.s: John Gabalas was a Byzantine Greek lord of Rhodes who succeeded his brother Leo Gabalas around 1240. Ruling under the loose overlordship of the Empire of Nicaea, he lost the island when the Genoese seized it in a surprise attack in 1248.

john-george-i-prince-of-anhalt-dessau.n: John George I, Prince of Anhalt-Dessau
john-george-i-prince-of-anhalt-dessau.s: John George I, Prince of Anhalt-Dessau, ruled the united principality of Anhalt with his brothers before its partition in 1603, when he received Dessau. He established the Calvinist principality of Anhalt-Dessau on the Mulde and Elbe, founding the line that later produced the…

john-george-i-duke-of-saxe-eisenach.n: John George I, Duke of Saxe-Eisenach
john-george-i-duke-of-saxe-eisenach.s: John George I, Duke of Saxe-Eisenach, was a son of Duke William of Saxe-Weimar and lord of Marksuhl. In 1672 he received Eisenach as a separate duchy, founding the line of Saxe-Eisenach that ruled until 1741.

john-graves-simcoe.s: John Graves Simcoe was a British army officer who commanded the Queen's Rangers in the American Revolutionary War. As the first lieutenant governor of Upper Canada from 1791 to 1796 he encouraged Loyalist settlement, laid out roads such as Yonge Street and moved the capital…

john-guy.s: John Guy was a Bristol merchant who led the first English attempt at permanent settlement in Newfoundland. In 1610 he founded the colony of Cupids on Conception Bay for the London and Bristol Company and served as its first governor.

john-hyrcanus.s: John Hyrcanus was Hasmonean high priest and ruler of Judea from 134 to 104 BCE, son of Simon Thassi. Taking advantage of Seleucid decline, he conquered Idumaea and forced its people to adopt Judaism, and destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim.

john-i-duke-of-brabant.s: John I, Duke of Brabant, ruled from 1267 to 1294 and was celebrated as a knightly hero and poet. After the line of Limburg ended in 1283 he claimed the duchy, and his victory at the Battle of Worringen in 1288 secured it for Brabant.

john-komnenos-asen.s: John Komnenos Asen was a Bulgarian noble and brother-in-law of the Serbian ruler Stefan Dušan, who made him governor of Valona and Kanina in Albania after taking them around 1345. After Dušan's death in 1355 he ruled them as an independent despot, also gaining Berat, until he…

john-ngu-foncha.s: John Ngu Foncha was a Cameroonian politician who led the Kamerun National Democratic Party and became premier of the British Southern Cameroons in 1959. He campaigned for reunification with French-speaking Cameroon, which the Southern Cameroons chose in the UN plebiscite of 1961.
